rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun about inheritance refers to blessings Israelites later acquired in Palestine, analogous to Egypt’s blessings, rather than the same Egyptian possessions.
rows.anchor: It actually refers to those favours and blessings the Israelites acquired in Palestine after setting out from Egypt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites received the fertile Palestinian land after leaving Egypt and finishing their desert wandering; history does not show that they occupied Egypt or its sphere.
rows.anchor: It is not proven from history that they were able to occupy any part of Egypt or areas under its sway.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the apparent reading points to the same orchards, fountains, and treasures, eloquent Arabic allows a pronoun to refer to analogous things.
rows.anchor: In eloquent Arabic, pronouns occur in this way as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’an 5:102 supplies a parallel: its pronoun alludes to questions like those Israelites asked, not the identical questions, supporting reference to similar blessings here.
rows.anchor: the same questions which the Israelites raised; similar questions are alluded to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the sea, the Israelites panicked and reproached Moses for bringing them into the desert to die, as also narrated in Exodus.
rows.anchor: Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us to the desert to die?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses reassured the Israelites that God was with them and would open a way, fulfilling His promise without allowing them harm.
rows.anchor: his Lord is with them and will open the way for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sea episode tested Moses’ and his nation’s trust in God: the Israelites failed as before, while Moses passed.
rows.anchor: the Israelites totally failed in it, but he passed it in flying colours.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A God-sent wind divided the sea; Moses and the Israelites crossed safely, Pharaoh’s army entered after them, and the returning water drowned it.
rows.anchor: the Pharaoh and his followers were faced with the ordeal of drowning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘huge mountain’ means a mountain of water; the Torah describes the same formation as a wall.
rows.anchor: The word “a huge mountain” of the verse refers to the mountain of water. In the Torah, the word “wall” has been used.

rows.speaker: Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī locates the Israelites’ sea crossing differently from the scholars of the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: The view of my mentor, Far āhī, regarding the place where the Israelites crossed into the sea is totally different

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi cannot assess Farāhī’s proposed crossing place because he does not know his arguments, and directs readers to Farāhī’s published Urdu collection.
rows.anchor: Since I am not aware of his arguments, I cannot say anything about this place with certainty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated closing verses frame the account as a sign containing many lessons for those who seek a sign.
rows.anchor: if these people want a sign, then this anecdote contains many lessons.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most people remain unwilling to believe even after witnessing the greatest signs, as happened with Pharaoh and his people.
rows.anchor: Even after observing the greatest of signs their majority is not inclined to accept faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can seize rebellious people through His might, yet His mercy gives them time to repent and reform.
rows.anchor: since He is also merciful, He also gives respite to people to repent and mend their ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Abraham narrative, like the preceding anecdote, serves the same preaching purpose and also ends with the recurring verses.
rows.anchor: the purpose of narrating this anecdote is the same as the one intended for the previous one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Abraham account fills the gap after Noah in the previous sūrah because Abraham was the most prominent messenger between Noah and Moses.
rows.anchor: the most prominent messenger between Noah (sws) and Moses (sws) was Abraham (sws).

none: Qur’an text and translation only; no commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s question is rhetorical, intended to discredit the people by exposing their worship as foolish and baseless.
rows.anchor: The question posed by Abraham (sws) was not meant to elicit an answer. It was meant to discredit his addressees.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people’s reply reflects arrogance and tribal bias.
rows.anchor: The answer of his people was punctuated by arrogance and by the bias they had for their tribal interests.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite Abraham’s repeated preaching, the people refuse to relinquish their deities.
rows.anchor: However much Abraham (sws) may emphasize his call, they will never give up their deities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s questions expose the idols’ baselessness; the people have no answer and persist only because they follow their forefathers, a tradition they will not abandon.
rows.anchor: because they are only following the ways of their forefathers, which they will not give up at any cost

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reported events occur after Abraham had conclusively conveyed the truth through both scriptural and intellectual arguments.
rows.anchor: when he had conclusively communicated the truth to his people through both scriptural and intellectual arguments
